intro: Every rule needs explaining. The Torah says rest on Shabbat, but it does not say what rest means. It says dwell in booths, but not how tall a booth should be. For hundreds of years, Jewish teachers passed explanations from one person to the next, out loud, by memory. Rabbinic tradition calls this the Oral Torah.

This unit follows that chain from Mount Sinai to a book. You will meet Ezra reading the Torah to a crowd, the Pharisees and Sadducees arguing about tradition, and Hillel and Shammai, who disagreed and are both remembered. Then you will watch a city burn, a rabbi escape in a coffin, and a scholar named Judah the Prince gather everything into the Mishnah.

By the end, you will be able to tell the Written Torah from the Oral Torah, name the six orders of the Mishnah, and explain why the rabbis kept the opinions that lost. You will also practice the course's habit: say who holds a belief, and describe what a text says without deciding whether it is true.
bigQuestion: How did the Oral Torah travel from memory to the Mishnah, and why did the rabbis write it down?

title: From Sinai to the Mishnah

chapters.title: Written Torah and Oral Torah
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Jewish teachers pass on the explanations of the Torah before anyone wrote them down?

story.title: The Chain of Remembering
story.kicker: One teacher tells one student, who tells the next, for hundreds of years.
paragraphs: Picture a long line of people. At the front stands a very old teacher. Jewish tradition calls him Moses. He turns to the person behind him and says the rules of the Torah out loud. He also explains what the rules mean. The person behind him listens hard and remembers every word.

That person grows up and becomes a teacher too. He turns to a student behind him and says the same words. He adds the same explanations. The line goes on and on. Each person is a student first, then a teacher. Nobody in the line writes the explanations down. They keep them by memory.

This is the story rabbinic tradition tells about the Oral Torah. The word oral means spoken. Rabbis in the Talmud say that Moses received two things at Mount Sinai. One was the Written Torah, the five books kept on a scroll. The other was the Oral Torah, the explanations that go with it.

The first chapter of Pirkei Avot, a book of the Mishnah, lists the chain. It names Moses, then Joshua, then the elders, then the prophets. Then it names the Men of the Great Assembly. After them come pairs of teachers, all the way to Hillel and Shammai. Jewish tradition holds that the chain never broke.

In this chapter you will walk along that chain. You will meet Ezra, who read the Torah aloud to a crowd. You will meet the Pharisees and the Sadducees, who argued about whether the Oral Torah was real. You will find out why a short rule, like rest on Shabbat, needed so much explaining.
story.think: Have you ever passed a message down a line of people? What helped the message stay the same, and what changed it?

lessons.title: The Torah on a Scroll
lessons.mainIdea: The Written Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, kept as a scroll and read aloud.
reading: The word *Torah* means teaching. In Jewish tradition it names the first five books of the Hebrew Bible. They are Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. They tell how the world began. They tell about Abraham's family. They tell how Moses led the people out of Egypt. They also hold many rules for daily life.

A *synagogue* is a Jewish house of worship. There the Torah is kept as a *scroll*. A scribe writes it by hand on long sheets of parchment. The sheets are sewn together. Then they are rolled around two wooden poles. On Shabbat and many other days, a reader unrolls the scroll. She or he chants a part of it aloud.

Rabbinic tradition calls this the Written Torah. It is written, so anyone who can read Hebrew can look at the words. The rabbis of the Talmud treated every word of it with care. They also noticed something. Many of its rules are short. A short rule leaves a lot of questions. That is where the next lesson begins.

words.d: the first five books of the Hebrew Bible; the word means teaching
a long roll of parchment with writing on it, rolled around two poles
a Jewish house of worship, prayer and study

look.title: Five Books in a Row
look.text: Imagine a shelf with five books on it. The first one starts with the making of the world. The second one tells about leaving Egypt and about Mount Sinai. The last one is Moses saying goodbye to the people. All five are copied onto one long scroll, with no pictures and no chapter numbers.
look.prompt: Why might reading a book aloud from a scroll feel different from reading it silently from a printed page?

check.q: What does the word Torah mean?
check.why: Torah means teaching. In Jewish tradition it names the first five books of the Hebrew Bible.

check.q: How many books are in the Written Torah?
check.why: The Written Torah is five books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Sixty-three is the number of tractates in the Mishnah.

check.q: How is the Torah kept in a synagogue?
choices: as a printed book with pictures
as a set of clay tablets
as a handwritten scroll on two poles
as a recording that is played aloud
check.why: A scribe writes the Torah by hand on parchment, and the sheets are rolled around two wooden poles to make a scroll.

lessons.title: The Torah That Was Spoken
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbinic tradition holds that Moses also received an Oral Torah, the explanations, which was passed on by memory.
reading: The Talmud tells of a second Torah. Rabbinic tradition holds that at Mount Sinai, Moses received the Written Torah and also an *Oral Torah*. Oral means spoken. The Oral Torah was the set of explanations that went with the written words. It told how to do what the Written Torah said.

According to this tradition, the Oral Torah was not written down for a very long time. A teacher said it to a student. The student learned it by heart. Then that student taught it to the next one. The rabbis called this passing on a *tradition*, something handed from one person to the next.

Not everyone reads this story the same way. Orthodox Jews hold that the Oral Torah truly came from Sinai. Many Conservative and Reform Jews see it as the wisdom of teachers over many centuries. Historians study when each part was written down. In this course we describe what the tradition says and how its readers understand it.

words.d: in rabbinic tradition, the spoken explanations of the Torah, passed on by memory before they were written down
a teaching or practice handed down from one person or generation to the next

look.title: The Chain Begins
look.text: The first mishnah of Pirkei Avot says that Moses received the Torah from Sinai and handed it on to Joshua. Joshua handed it to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the Men of the Great Assembly. Those men taught three things: be careful when you judge, raise up many students, and make a fence around the Torah.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 1:1, retold from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Why do you think the text lists who received the teaching, one after another?

check.q: What does the word oral mean?
check.why: Oral means spoken. The Oral Torah, in rabbinic tradition, was passed on by speaking and memory.

check.q: According to rabbinic tradition, what is the Oral Torah?
choices: the explanations of the Written Torah
the last five books of the Bible
a song sung at Mount Sinai
check.why: Rabbinic tradition holds that the Oral Torah is the set of explanations that tells how to carry out the Written Torah.

check.q: How do Orthodox Jews and many Reform Jews read the story of the Oral Torah differently?
choices: Both say it was never taught at all
Orthodox Jews hold it came from Sinai; many Reform Jews see it as teachers' wisdom over centuries
Reform Jews hold it came from Sinai; Orthodox Jews say it was invented
Both agree it was written down at Sinai
check.why: Orthodox tradition holds the Oral Torah came from Sinai. Many Conservative and Reform readers see it as the work of teachers over many generations.

lessons.title: Why a Rule Needs Explaining
lessons.mainIdea: Short rules like rest on Shabbat raise questions, and the Oral Torah is where the rabbis worked out answers.
reading: The Written Torah says to remember *Shabbat*, the seventh day, and keep it holy. It says not to do any work on that day. That sounds simple. But try to use the rule. Is cooking work? Is carrying a book work? Is walking to a friend's house work? The Torah does not give a list.

The rabbis said the Oral Torah answers these questions. The Mishnah, in tractate Shabbat, lists thirty-nine kinds of work. Planting, baking, sewing and writing are on the list. So is carrying from one place to another. Jewish tradition links them to building the *tabernacle*, the tent of worship in the desert.

This is the pattern for the whole course. A short rule in the Written Torah leads to a *question*. The question leads to a discussion. The discussion leads to a ruling, and often to a second opinion that is kept too. The rabbis believed that asking a good question was a way of honoring the Torah.

words.d: the seventh day of the week, a day of rest in Jewish tradition, from Friday evening to Saturday night
something asked to find out what a rule means or how to use it
the tent of worship the Israelites carried in the desert, according to the Torah

look.title: Remember the Seventh Day
look.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
look.prompt: This verse is nine words long. Name two questions a person might ask before they could follow it.

check.q: Which of these is a question the Written Torah does not answer on its own?
choices: Does carrying a book count as work?
check.why: The Torah says not to work on Shabbat but gives no list of what counts. The rabbis worked out that question in the Oral Torah.

check.q: How many kinds of work does the Mishnah in tractate Shabbat list?
check.why: Mishnah Shabbat lists thirty-nine kinds of work, which tradition links to building the tabernacle.

check.q: In this course, what usually comes right after a short rule from the Written Torah?
choices: a question about what it means
check.why: The pattern is rule, question, discussion, ruling. A good question is how the rabbis began their work.

lessons.title: Ezra Reads to the Crowd
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible tells that Ezra read the Torah aloud to the people, and helpers explained it, around 450 BCE.
reading: Long before the Talmud, the Jewish people came home from *exile* in Babylon. Their first Temple in Jerusalem had been destroyed. They built a second one. Then a scribe named *Ezra* came from Babylon. The Bible says he had set his heart on studying the Torah and teaching it.

The book of Nehemiah tells what happened next. Ezra stood on a wooden platform in a square in Jerusalem. He opened the scroll, and the whole crowd stood up. He read from morning until midday. Men, women and children old enough to understand were there. Helpers stood among the people and explained the reading so everyone understood.

Historians date this reading to about 450 BCE, though the exact year is debated. Rabbinic tradition loves this scene. It shows the Written Torah being read aloud and the meaning being explained at the same time. To the rabbis, Ezra looked like one of them. Later teachers said that if Moses had not come first, Ezra would have been worthy to receive the Torah.

words.d: a scribe and teacher who, the Bible says, read the Torah aloud in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon
being forced to live far from your homeland
a person whose job is to copy and study written texts

look.title: Reading with the Meaning
look.text: The book of Nehemiah says that they read from the book of the Torah of God clearly. They gave the sense, so that the people understood what was being read.
look.cite: Nehemiah 8:8, retold from the JPS Tanakh, 1917
look.prompt: What is the difference between reading words aloud and giving the sense of them?

check.q: Where did Ezra come from before he read the Torah in Jerusalem?
check.why: Ezra came from Babylon, where many Jews had lived in exile after the first Temple was destroyed.

check.q: What did the helpers do while Ezra read?
choices: They explained the reading so people understood
check.why: Nehemiah 8 says helpers gave the sense of the reading so the people understood it.

check.q: About when do historians date Ezra's reading?
check.why: Historians place Ezra's reading around 450 BCE, in the time of the Second Temple. The exact year is debated.

lessons.title: The Men of the Great Assembly
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbinic tradition names a group after Ezra, the Men of the Great Assembly, as a link in the chain of teachers.
reading: Pirkei Avot lists the chain of teachers. After the prophets, it names the *Men of the Great Assembly*. Rabbinic tradition pictures them as a large council of scholars in the time of Ezra and after. The tradition holds that they kept the Oral Torah alive and helped shape Jewish prayer.

Avot says the Men of the Great Assembly taught three sayings. Be careful in judgment. Raise up many students, called disciples. Make a fence around the Torah. A fence is a rule that keeps you a safe step away from breaking a bigger rule. For example, a fence might say to stop work a little before Shabbat begins.

Historians know very little about this group. The Talmud and the Mishnah are the main places it is described. So some scholars treat the Great Assembly as a name for the many teachers of that time. Jewish tradition, in turn, treats it as a real council. In this course, both readings are worth knowing.

words.d: in rabbinic tradition, a council of teachers after Ezra who passed on the Torah and its explanations
a student who learns closely from a teacher
in rabbinic law, an extra rule that keeps a person a safe distance from breaking a Torah rule

look.title: A Fence Around a Rule
look.text: A school rule says: do not run in the hall. A teacher adds a second rule: walk on the right side of the hall. The second rule is not the same as the first. But it makes the first one easier to keep. Rabbinic tradition calls a rule like the second one a fence around the Torah.
look.prompt: Think of one rule at home or school and invent a fence that would help people keep it.

check.q: What is a fence around the Torah?
choices: an extra rule that keeps a person from breaking a Torah rule
a wall built around a synagogue
a scroll kept in a locked box
a line of students waiting to read
check.why: In rabbinic tradition, a fence is an added rule that keeps a person a safe step away from breaking a Torah rule.

check.q: Where is the saying of the Men of the Great Assembly found?
check.why: Pirkei Avot 1:1 lists the chain of teachers and the three sayings of the Men of the Great Assembly.

check.q: How do many historians see the Men of the Great Assembly?
choices: as a group described only in Greek books
as the writers of the book of Genesis
as a name for the many teachers of that time, since little is known
as the first rabbis in Babylon
check.why: Little is known outside rabbinic texts, so some historians read the Great Assembly as a name for the teachers of that era. Tradition treats it as a real council.

lessons.title: The Second Temple
lessons.mainIdea: The Second Temple in Jerusalem stood for about 500 years and was the center of Jewish worship while the Oral Torah was passed on.
reading: The *Temple* was the great house of worship in Jerusalem. Jewish tradition says King Solomon built the first one. The Babylonians destroyed it in 586 BCE. When the people came home, they built a second one. Historians date its finishing to about 515 BCE. It was later made much larger by King Herod.

In the Second Temple, priests offered gifts of animals, grain and wine. Each gift was a sacrifice. People came from far away for three big festivals each year. Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot all brought crowds to Jerusalem. The Torah gave rules for each festival, and the Oral Torah, tradition holds, explained how to keep them.

The Second Temple stood for about five hundred years. During those years the chain of teachers went on. The Written Torah was read. The Oral Torah was taught. Different Jewish groups grew up in Jerusalem, and they did not all agree. The next section meets two of them.

words.d: the central house of worship in ancient Jerusalem; the second one stood from c. 515 BCE to 70 CE
a gift of an animal, grain or wine offered to God at the Temple
a yearly holiday; the Torah names Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot as times to go to Jerusalem

look.title: The Temples in Time
look.cite: dates as commonly given by historians; Ezra's year is approximate
look.prompt: About how many years did the Second Temple stand? Show how you worked it out.

check.q: Who destroyed the First Temple, and when?
check.why: The Babylonians destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE. Rome destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE.

check.q: What happened at the Temple that could not happen anywhere else?
check.why: Sacrifices of animals, grain and wine were offered by priests at the Temple in Jerusalem.

check.q: Which three festivals brought crowds to Jerusalem?
check.why: The Torah names Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot as the three times to go up to Jerusalem.

sections.title: Who Believed in the Oral Torah?

lessons.title: Pharisees and Sadducees
lessons.mainIdea: In the time of the Second Temple, the Pharisees accepted the Oral Torah and the Sadducees did not.
reading: Near the end of the Second Temple period, several Jewish groups lived in the Land of Israel. Two of them argued about the Oral Torah. The *Pharisees* taught that the traditions handed down from the elders were part of God's teaching. The *Sadducees* said that only the Written Torah counted.

The Jewish historian Josephus, who lived in the first century CE, wrote about both groups. He says the Pharisees followed many rules passed down from their ancestors that were not written in the Torah of Moses. He says the Sadducees rejected those rules. Many Sadducees were priests and wealthy families. Many Pharisees were teachers of ordinary people.

When the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE, the Sadducees lost their center. The Pharisees' way of study continued. The rabbis of the Mishnah and Talmud saw themselves as heirs of the Pharisees. That is one reason the Talmud is full of the Oral Torah, the traditions the Pharisees had defended.

words.d: a Jewish group in the Second Temple period that accepted the traditions of the elders, the Oral Torah
a Jewish group in the Second Temple period, many of them priests, that accepted only the Written Torah
a Jewish historian of the first century CE who wrote about the groups of his time

look.title: Two Answers to One Question
look.text: Someone asks: how do we know what counts as work on Shabbat? A Sadducee answers: read the Torah; what is written is all we have. A Pharisee answers: our teachers received explanations from their teachers, and those explanations tell us. Both are pointing to the Torah. They disagree about where its meaning comes from.
look.prompt: Put each answer in your own words. What does each side think a person needs in order to keep the rule?

check.q: Which group accepted the Oral Torah?
check.why: The Pharisees held that the traditions of the elders were part of the Torah. The Sadducees accepted only what was written.

check.q: Who was Josephus?
choices: a Sadducee priest who wrote the Mishnah
a Jewish historian of the first century CE
check.why: Josephus was a Jewish historian of the first century CE. His books describe the Pharisees, Sadducees and other groups.

check.q: Why does the Talmud contain so much Oral Torah?
choices: The rabbis saw themselves as heirs of the Pharisees, who defended it
check.why: The rabbis of the Mishnah and Talmud saw themselves as continuing the Pharisees' way, which accepted the traditions of the elders.

lessons.title: Hillel and Shammai
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel and Shammai, two teachers around the end of the first century BCE, were the last pair in the chain named in Avot.
reading: Pirkei Avot names five *pairs* of teachers after the Men of the Great Assembly. The last pair is *Hillel* and *Shammai*. Historians place them around the end of the first century BCE, when Herod was king. Tradition says Hillel came from Babylon to study in Jerusalem and became a leading teacher there.

The Talmud tells many stories about the two. Hillel is shown as patient and gentle. Shammai is shown as strict and quick. In one story, a man asks each of them to teach the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Shammai sends him away. Hillel says: what is hateful to you, do not do to another; the rest is explanation, go and learn.

Each teacher had students. Their students formed two schools, the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai. The schools disagreed on hundreds of rules. The Mishnah records both sides. Rabbinic tradition holds that the law usually follows the House of Hillel, but it keeps the House of Shammai's view on the page too.

words.d: a teacher in Jerusalem around the end of the first century BCE, known for patience; head of the House of Hillel
Hillel's partner in the chain of teachers, known for strictness; head of the House of Shammai
the five sets of two teachers that Pirkei Avot names between the Great Assembly and the Mishnah

look.title: Hillel's Sayings
look.text: Pirkei Avot records Hillel saying: be one of the students of Aaron, who loved peace and chased after peace, who loved people and drew them near to the Torah. Hillel also said: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 1:12 and 1:14, retold from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Pick one of Hillel's sayings. Tell what it asks a person to do.

check.q: About when did Hillel and Shammai teach?
choices: around the end of the first century BCE
check.why: Historians place Hillel and Shammai around the end of the first century BCE, when Herod ruled. Rabbi Judah the Prince came c. 200 CE.

check.q: In the story of the man on one foot, what did Hillel do?
choices: He told him to come back next year
He gave him one rule and told him to go and learn
check.why: Hillel answered: what is hateful to you, do not do to another; the rest is explanation, go and learn. Shammai is the one who sent the man away.

check.q: What does the Mishnah do with the House of Shammai's opinions?
choices: It blames them for the Temple's fall
It says they are always right
It records them next to the House of Hillel's
check.why: The Mishnah keeps both houses' views. Tradition holds that the law usually follows Hillel, but Shammai's side stays on the page.

lessons.title: How to Keep a Holiday
lessons.mainIdea: The Oral Torah explains how to keep the Torah's holidays, and the rabbis' disagreements about them are part of the tradition.
reading: The Written Torah names holidays but leaves out many details. It says to dwell in booths on *Sukkot* for seven days. It does not say how big a booth must be. It does not say what the roof is made of. It says to eat unleavened bread on *Passover*. It does not say what to do with bread you forgot in a cupboard.

The Mishnah fills in the details. Tractate Sukkah begins with how tall a booth may be. The Houses of Hillel and Shammai even argue about a booth's roof. Tractate Pesachim tells how to search the house for leavened bread. This happens the night before Passover, by the light of a lamp.

This is how the Oral Torah worked, as rabbinic tradition tells it. Rules were passed down, questions were asked, and answers were argued. The details were still in memory when the Second Temple fell. In the next chapter, a rabbi carried out of a burning city helps keep them from being lost.

words.d: a fall festival when, the Torah says, people dwell in booths for seven days
a spring festival that remembers leaving Egypt; the Torah says to eat unleavened bread
one book of the Mishnah or Talmud on one subject, such as Sukkah or Pesachim

look.title: How Tall Is a Booth?
look.text: The Mishnah says that a sukkah, a festival booth, that is taller than twenty cubits is not fit for use. Rabbi Judah says it is fit. A booth that is not ten handbreadths tall is also not fit. A cubit is about the length from the elbow to the fingertips.
look.cite: Mishnah Sukkah 1:1, paraphrased from the Hebrew Mishnah
look.prompt: The Torah says dwell in booths. Why do you think the Mishnah starts with how tall a booth may be?

check.q: What does the Written Torah say to do on Sukkot?
choices: dwell in booths for seven days
search the house with a lamp
check.why: The Torah says to dwell in booths on Sukkot. The Mishnah in tractate Sukkah adds the details.

check.q: Which tractate tells how to search for leavened bread before Passover?
check.why: Tractate Pesachim is about Passover. It describes searching the house for leavened bread by lamplight.

check.q: What does Rabbi Judah say about a booth taller than twenty cubits?
check.why: Mishnah Sukkah 1:1 says such a booth is not fit, and then records Rabbi Judah's view that it is fit. Both views are kept.

review.q: In rabbinic tradition, what two things did Moses receive at Sinai?
choices: the books of Ezra and Nehemiah
the Written Torah and the Oral Torah
review.why: Rabbinic tradition holds that Moses received the Written Torah and, along with it, the spoken explanations called the Oral Torah.

review.q: Which book of the Mishnah lists the chain of teachers from Moses onward?
review.why: Pirkei Avot 1:1 begins with Moses receiving the Torah and passing it on, link by link.

review.q: What did Ezra do in the square in Jerusalem?
choices: He read the Torah aloud while helpers explained it
review.why: Nehemiah 8 tells that Ezra read the Torah aloud from morning to midday, and helpers gave the sense.

Because it says no work but does not list what counts
Because only priests could read it
review.why: The Torah says not to work on Shabbat. What counts as work is worked out in the Oral Torah and listed in the Mishnah.

review.q: Which group accepted only the Written Torah?
review.why: The Sadducees rejected the traditions of the elders. The Pharisees, and later the rabbis, accepted the Oral Torah.

choices: the last pair of teachers named in the chain in Avot
two priests at the First Temple
the writers of the book of Nehemiah
review.why: Hillel and Shammai are the last of the five pairs Pirkei Avot names, around the end of the first century BCE.

review.q: What is a fence around the Torah?
choices: a stone wall around the Temple
an extra rule that keeps a person from breaking a bigger rule
a box that holds a scroll
a list of thirty-nine kinds of work
review.why: The Men of the Great Assembly, Avot says, taught to make a fence around the Torah: an added rule that guards a Torah rule.

choices: a scroll kept in a synagogue
one book of the Mishnah or Talmud on one subject
review.why: A tractate is one book of the Mishnah or Talmud on a single subject, such as Sukkah or Pesachim.

chapters.title: Judah the Prince Writes It Down
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did the rabbis gather the Oral Torah into the Mishnah, and what does the Mishnah look like?

story.title: A Coffin and a Question
story.kicker: A rabbi leaves a city under siege the only way the guards will let him: as a dead man.
paragraphs: The year is 70 CE. Roman soldiers surround Jerusalem. Inside the walls, people are hungry, and fighters will not let anyone leave. A teacher named Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai wants to get out. He believes the city will fall. He wants to save something before it does.

The Talmud, in tractate Gittin, tells how he did it. His students spread the word that their teacher had died. They laid him in a coffin. Two of them, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua, carried it toward the gate. The guards wanted to check with a sword. The students said: do you want the Romans to say Jews stab their own teachers? The guards let the coffin pass.

Outside the walls, the rabbi climbed out. He asked to see the Roman general, Vespasian. The story says he greeted the general as a king. Vespasian was not yet emperor, so he was annoyed. Just then a messenger arrived from Rome with news: the old emperor was dead, and Vespasian was to take his place.

The general said the rabbi could ask for something. Rabbi Yochanan did not ask for the city. He asked for Yavneh and its scholars, a small town where teachers could keep studying. He asked for the family of Rabban Gamliel to be spared. He asked for a doctor for a sick rabbi. Vespasian said yes.

That is how the Talmud remembers it. Historians say the story grew in the telling, but Yavneh really did become the center of Jewish learning after the Temple burned. In this chapter you will see what the teachers at Yavneh feared, and how, about 130 years later, Rabbi Judah the Prince answered that fear with a book.
story.think: The rabbi could have asked the general for anything. Why do you think he asked for a school?

lessons.title: Rome Burns the Temple
lessons.mainIdea: In 70 CE the Roman army destroyed the Second Temple, and Jewish life had to find a new center.
reading: For about a hundred years, *Rome* had ruled the Land of Israel. Roman governors taxed the people and put down protests. In 66 CE a *revolt* broke out. Jewish fighters drove out the Roman soldiers. Rome sent a large army. The general Vespasian led it, and later his son Titus.

In the summer of 70 CE, after a long *siege*, Roman soldiers broke into Jerusalem. They set fire to the Temple. Jewish tradition remembers that day with a fast. It falls on the ninth of the month of Av. The historian Josephus was there with the Roman side. He wrote a long account of the fall of the city.

The Temple had been the center of Jewish worship. Sacrifices could only be offered there. Now it was gone. Rabbinic tradition tells that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai comforted a student who wept at the ruins. He said that acts of kindness could also bring people close to God. Prayer, study and kindness became the heart of Jewish life.

words.d: the empire that ruled the Land of Israel from 63 BCE and destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE
a fight by a people against the rulers over them
when an army surrounds a city so that nothing can go in or out

look.title: Two Ways to Be Close
look.text: A student stands at the burned Temple and cries. He says the place where sins were forgiven is gone. His teacher says: do not be sad; we have another way that is just as good, acts of kindness. Rabbinic tradition, in a book called Avot de-Rabbi Natan, tells this story about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.
look.prompt: What is the teacher trying to give his student in place of the Temple?

check.q: Which empire destroyed the Second Temple, and when?
check.why: The Roman army under Titus burned the Second Temple in the summer of 70 CE. Babylon destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE.

check.q: How does Jewish tradition remember the day the Temple burned?
choices: with a fast on the ninth of Av
check.why: The fast of the ninth of Av marks the destruction of the Temple in Jewish tradition.

check.q: What did Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai tell his weeping student?
choices: The Temple will be rebuilt next year
Acts of kindness can also bring people close to God
check.why: In the story told in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, the teacher says acts of kindness can take the place of the Temple's offerings.

lessons.title: Yavneh, a Town of Scholars
lessons.mainIdea: At Yavneh, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his students rebuilt Jewish teaching around study and prayer.
reading: *Yavneh* was a small town near the coast, south of today's Tel Aviv. After 70 CE it became a center of Jewish learning. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai taught there. His students, and their students, are the first rabbis whose names fill the Mishnah. The word *rabbi* means my teacher.

The teachers at Yavneh made rules for a world without a Temple. Tradition says Rabban Yochanan made a ruling about the shofar, a ram's horn. It could be blown on Rosh Hashanah at Yavneh, as it once was in the Temple. Later, Rabban Gamliel led the school. Tradition holds that he helped set the order of daily prayer.

Historians see Yavneh as the start of *rabbinic Judaism*, the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teaching. The Talmud tells its story with legends and details. What historians can say for sure is smaller. Both views agree that after the Temple fell, study and prayer became central.

words.d: a town in the Land of Israel that became the center of Jewish teaching after 70 CE
a Jewish teacher of Torah; the word means my teacher
the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teachings, the Mishnah and the Talmud

look.title: Yochanan's Request
look.text: The Talmud tells that when the general said Rabban Yochanan could ask for something, he asked for three things. Give me Yavneh and its sages. Spare the family line of Rabban Gamliel. And send doctors to heal Rabbi Zadok, who had fasted for many years.
look.cite: Gittin 56b, paraphrased from the Babylonian Talmud
look.prompt: Each request saves something. What does each one save?

check.q: What does the word rabbi mean?
check.why: Rabbi means my teacher. The teachers at Yavneh are the first rabbis named in the Mishnah.

check.q: Where was Yavneh?
choices: in the Land of Israel, near the coast
check.why: Yavneh was a small town near the coast of the Land of Israel, south of today's Tel Aviv.

check.q: What do historians mean by rabbinic Judaism?
choices: Judaism of the priests at the Temple
the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teaching
a group that rejected the Oral Torah
check.why: Rabbinic Judaism is the form of Judaism built on the rabbis' teachings, beginning at Yavneh and set down in the Mishnah and Talmud.

lessons.title: The Fear of Forgetting
lessons.mainIdea: War and persecution made the rabbis fear the Oral Torah would be forgotten, and that fear pushed them to gather it.
reading: The Oral Torah lived in *memory*. Every teacher held a piece of it. If a teacher died before passing it on, that piece could be lost. In the years after 70 CE, many teachers died. War, hunger and Roman punishment took them. The rabbis began to worry.

In 132 CE a second revolt broke out, led by Simon *Bar Kokhba*. It lasted about three years and ended in defeat. Rabbinic tradition says Rome then forbade the teaching of Torah. It tells that Rabbi Akiva kept teaching and was put to death. Many of his students died too. The rabbis moved north to the Galilee, to towns like Usha.

The teachers who survived did something new. They began to gather the teachings into short, clear sayings that could be learned by heart. Each saying was called a *mishnah*, from a Hebrew word for repeating. Students repeated them until they knew them cold. These collections became the raw material for the book you meet next.

words.d: the power to hold and repeat what you have learned
the leader of a Jewish revolt against Rome from 132 to 135 CE
as a small word, one short teaching learned by repeating; as a book, the Mishnah, the whole collection

look.title: Losses and Moves
rows: Revolt defeated; rabbis move to the Galilee
Mishnah gathered by Rabbi Judah the Prince (about)
look.cite: dates as commonly given by historians; the Mishnah's date is approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Temple's fall and the Mishnah? What could be forgotten in that time?

check.q: Why did the rabbis fear the Oral Torah would be lost?
choices: Because it was written in Greek
Because it lived in memory and many teachers were dying
Because the Sadducees had hidden it
check.why: The Oral Torah was held in memory. When war and persecution killed teachers, their pieces of it could be lost.

check.q: When was the Bar Kokhba revolt?
check.why: Bar Kokhba led a revolt against Rome from 132 to 135 CE. The first revolt ended in 70 CE.

check.q: What does the word mishnah come from?
check.why: Mishnah comes from a Hebrew root meaning to repeat. Students learned each teaching by repeating it.

lessons.title: The Man Called Rabbi
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Judah the Prince, leader of the Jews in the Land of Israel around 200 CE, gathered the Oral Torah into the Mishnah.
reading: *Judah the Prince* was born, tradition says, around the time of the Bar Kokhba revolt. He came from the family of Hillel. He became the *Nasi*, the prince or leader of the Jewish community under Roman rule. He was wealthy, respected by Roman officials, and a great scholar. The Talmud calls him simply Rabbi, the teacher.

Rabbi Judah lived in the Galilee, first in Bet She'arim and later in Sepphoris. He gathered the teachings of the earlier rabbis, the tannaim. He sorted them by subject. He chose which sayings to keep and how to word them. He kept many disagreements, naming who said what. Historians date the finished Mishnah to about 200 CE.

Was the Mishnah written on a scroll or held in memory? Scholars debate this. Some say Rabbi Judah arranged it to be memorized. Others say it was written down early. Either way, from about 200 CE on, the Mishnah was a fixed text. Every rabbi after him studied the same six orders in the same words.

words.d: the rabbi who gathered the Mishnah, c. 200 CE; the Talmud calls him Rabbi
the prince, the leader of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel under Rome
the rabbis whose teachings are in the Mishnah, from about 10 to 220 CE

look.title: Rabbi's Own Saying
look.text: Pirkei Avot records a saying of Rabbi, that is, Judah the Prince. He asked: which is the right path for a person to choose? One that brings honor to the one who walks it and honor from other people. He also said: be as careful with a small mitzvah as with a big one, since you do not know the reward for each.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 2:1, retold from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Why might a person be tempted to treat a small rule less carefully than a big one?

check.q: What title does the Talmud give Judah the Prince?
check.why: The Talmud calls Judah the Prince simply Rabbi, the teacher. Ezra is the one called the scribe.

check.q: What does Nasi mean?
choices: the prince or leader of the Jewish community
check.why: Nasi means prince. It was the title of the leader of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel under Rome.

check.q: About when was the Mishnah finished?
check.why: Historians date the Mishnah to about 200 CE, in the time of Rabbi Judah the Prince.

lessons.title: Six Orders on a Shelf
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah is arranged in six orders by subject, and each order holds several tractates.
reading: The Mishnah is sorted into six orders. In Hebrew each *order* is a seder, the same word used for the Passover meal. The orders are Seeds, Festivals, Women, Damages, Holy Things and Purities. Together they hold sixty-three tractates, or books, each on one subject.

Seeds is about farming and blessings. Festivals is about Shabbat and the holidays. Women is about marriage and family. *Damages* is about courts, money, harm and fairness. Holy Things is about the Temple and its offerings. Purities is about what is clean and unclean for Temple purposes. Pirkei Avot sits inside the order of Damages.

The orders show what the rabbis cared about. Two whole orders are about a Temple that no longer stood. The rabbis kept studying its rules anyway. Jewish tradition holds that studying the rules counts as a kind of keeping them. Historians see it as a way of keeping the Temple alive in memory.

words.d: one of the six big parts of the Mishnah; in Hebrew, seder
the order of the Mishnah about courts, money, harm and fairness; Pirkei Avot is inside it

look.title: Tractates in Each Order
look.cite: the standard count of the Mishnah's 63 tractates
look.prompt: Add the six numbers. Which order has the fewest tractates, and what is it about?

check.q: How many orders does the Mishnah have?
check.why: The Mishnah has six orders. Sixty-three is the number of tractates inside them.

check.q: Which order holds Pirkei Avot?
check.why: Pirkei Avot is a tractate in the order of Damages, next to the tractates about courts.

check.q: Which order is about Shabbat and the holidays?
check.why: The order of Festivals covers Shabbat, Passover, Sukkot and the other holidays.

lessons.title: Short, Clear and in Hebrew
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah is written in short Hebrew sentences that state rules and record who disagreed.
reading: Open the Mishnah and you find short sentences. Each one states a rule or a case. The language is *Hebrew*, a plain and clear Hebrew that scholars call Mishnaic Hebrew. There is very little story and very little explaining. The Mishnah says what the rule is. It rarely says why.

The Mishnah also records *disagreement*. A rule will be stated, and then: Rabbi Judah says otherwise. Or: the House of Shammai say this, and the House of Hillel say that. The first tractate, Berakhot, starts with a question about when to say the evening Shema. Three answers are given, from three teachers.

Why keep the losing side? Rabbinic tradition gives an answer in the Mishnah itself. It says a court might one day agree with the lost opinion, so it must be on the page. The Mishnah is short because it was made to be remembered. It keeps the arguments because, to the rabbis, the arguing was part of the Torah.

words.d: the language of the Torah and the Mishnah
when two teachers give different answers to the same question; the Mishnah records both
a prayer from the Torah beginning Hear, O Israel, said in the morning and evening

look.title: The Mishnah's First Lines
look.text: The Mishnah opens by asking from what time the evening Shema may be recited. It answers: from the hour when the priests go in to eat their offering, until the end of the first watch of the night. That is the view of Rabbi Eliezer. The sages say until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until the dawn comes up.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, paraphrased from the Hebrew Mishnah
look.prompt: Count the answers in this one mishnah. Why do you think the text gives all of them instead of just one?

check.q: In what language is the Mishnah written?
check.why: The Mishnah is in a plain, clear Hebrew. The Gemara, which came later, is mostly in Aramaic.

check.q: What is the first question in the Mishnah?
choices: When may the evening Shema be recited?
How tall may a sukkah be?
What counts as work on Shabbat?
Who received the Torah at Sinai?
check.why: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 asks from what time the evening Shema may be said, and gives three answers.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah keep an opinion that did not win?
choices: Because a later court might agree with it
Because the losing side wrote the book
check.why: The Mishnah says a later court might side with the lost opinion, so it stays on the page. The arguing was part of the tradition.

lessons.title: A Book That Asks for More
lessons.mainIdea: Because the Mishnah states rules without reasons, later rabbis kept asking why, and their discussion became the Gemara.
reading: The Mishnah solved one problem and made another. The Oral Torah was now safe in a fixed text. But the text was short. It said what the rule was, not why. A student who read that the evening Shema is said when the priests go in to eat would ask: why the priests? What time is that?

So the rabbis after Rabbi Judah studied the Mishnah the way earlier rabbis had studied the Torah. They asked what each line meant. They compared one mishnah to another. They brought in old teachings that were left out of the Mishnah. Each one is called a *baraita*. This discussion, in the Land of Israel and in Babylon, went on for about three hundred years.

That discussion is the *Gemara*. The word means completion or learning in Aramaic. Mishnah plus Gemara equals *Talmud*. So the Mishnah is like a seed. The Gemara grew from it, and the Talmud is the whole tree. The next unit follows that growing.

words.d: the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah, gathered c. 400 to 500 CE; with the Mishnah it makes the Talmud
the Mishnah together with the Gemara; the word means learning
a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in it; plural, baraitot

look.title: From Seed to Tree
look.text: Picture a page. In the middle is a short paragraph in Hebrew: the Mishnah. Around it grows a much longer text in Aramaic: the Gemara, asking what the short paragraph means. Around that, in smaller print, grow later explanations. The short paragraph in the middle is about the size of your hand. The page is as big as a tray.
look.prompt: Why would a short, clear rule book lead to a much longer book of discussion?

check.q: What is the Gemara?
choices: the six orders of the Mishnah
the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah
check.why: The Gemara is the discussion of the Mishnah by later rabbis. Together, Mishnah and Gemara make up the Talmud.

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: a teaching from the Mishnah's time that was left out of the Mishnah
check.why: A baraita is an early teaching not included in the Mishnah. The Gemara often brings baraitot into its discussion.

check.q: Mishnah plus Gemara equals what?
check.why: The Talmud is the Mishnah together with the Gemara. Torah is the five books; Avot is one tractate.

lessons.title: What the Mishnah Protects
lessons.mainIdea: Many of the Mishnah's rules protect people who could be hurt: the worker, the poor, the stranger and the person on trial.
reading: The Mishnah is not only about Temple and festival. Much of it is about fairness between people. In the order of Damages, one tractate says that a *worker* must be paid on time. Another is about lost objects. If a lost thing has a sign on it, the finder must announce it. Then the owner can claim it.

The order of Seeds has a rule for farmers. Leave the corners of the field for the *poor* and the *stranger*. This comes from the Torah. The Mishnah works out how big a corner should be. It treats these gifts as the poor person's right, not just as kindness.

Tractate Sanhedrin, about courts, is careful with people on trial. When a life is at stake, it says, witnesses must be warned first. One person, it says, is like a whole world. Rabbinic tradition reads these rules as *mercy* built into law. In this course, mercy and argument are the two threads to follow.

words.d: a person paid to do a job; the Mishnah says a worker must be paid on time
a person from somewhere else who lives among you; the Torah and Mishnah give the stranger a share of the harvest
care for someone who is weak, in trouble or in your power
people who do not have enough; the Mishnah gives them a right to the corners of the field

look.title: One Life, One World
look.text: Mishnah Sanhedrin says that a person was created alone at the beginning to teach that whoever destroys one life is counted as if he destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life is counted as if he saved a whole world. Some old copies of the Mishnah read one life of Israel; others read simply one life.
look.cite: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, paraphrased from the Hebrew Mishnah
look.prompt: This is said to witnesses before a trial for a person's life. Why would a court want witnesses to hear it first?

check.q: What does the Mishnah say about paying a worker?
choices: Pay only at the end of the year
Pay only if the work is perfect
check.why: The Mishnah, following the Torah, says a worker must be paid on time. This protects the worker.

check.q: Who gets the corners of the field, according to the Torah and Mishnah?
check.why: The Torah says to leave the corners for the poor and the stranger. The Mishnah in Seeds works out the details.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah say a person was created alone?
choices: To show that each life is like a whole world
To show that people should live alone
To explain why there are six orders
To warn against building a sukkah
check.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 says one person was created first to teach that each life counts as a whole world.

lessons.title: Two Chapters, One Chain
lessons.mainIdea: From Sinai to the Mishnah, rabbinic tradition tells one long chain of passing on and writing down.
reading: Look back at the two chapters of this unit. In rabbinic tradition, the *chain* starts with Moses at Sinai. It runs through Joshua, the elders, the prophets, the Men of the Great Assembly and the pairs. It reaches Hillel and Shammai. Then it reaches the teachers of Yavneh and, at last, Rabbi Judah the Prince.

Along that chain, the Oral Torah was spoken and remembered. Ezra read the Written Torah aloud and had it explained. The Pharisees defended the traditions of the elders. The Temple fell, and the rabbis feared forgetting. So Rabbi Judah gathered the teachings into a short, clear book: the Mishnah, c. 200 CE.

Different readers tell this chain differently. Orthodox tradition holds that every link goes back to Sinai. Many Conservative and Reform readers see a growing tradition shaped by people in each age. Historians test each link against evidence. All of them agree that the Mishnah became the *foundation* for everything the Talmud built next.

words.d: the line of teachers, each passing the tradition to the next, that Pirkei Avot describes
the base that everything else is built on

look.title: Links in a Line
look.text: Moses. Joshua. The elders. The prophets. The Men of the Great Assembly. Five pairs, ending with Hillel and Shammai. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. Rabban Gamliel. Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Judah the Prince. Some of these are people, some are groups, and some of the dates are guesses. That is how Pirkei Avot lays out the chain.
look.prompt: Pick one link and say what you learned about it in this unit. Which link would a historian want more evidence for?

check.q: Which of these comes last in the chain?
choices: the Men of the Great Assembly
check.why: Rabbi Judah the Prince, c. 200 CE, gathered the Mishnah. The other links come before him.

check.q: What did the rabbis fear after the Temple fell?
choices: that the Oral Torah would be forgotten
that the Mishnah was too long
check.why: With teachers dying in war and persecution, the rabbis feared the Oral Torah held in memory would be lost. The Mishnah was the answer.

check.q: How do historians treat the chain of teachers?
choices: They say every link is certain
They test each link against evidence
They say the chain was invented by Rome
They only study the Written Torah
check.why: Historians check each link against evidence and say when a date is uncertain. Jewish traditions read the chain in their own ways.

review.q: How did Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai leave Jerusalem, according to the Talmud?
choices: in a coffin carried by his students
review.why: Gittin 56a–b tells that his students carried him out in a coffin, telling the guards he had died.

review.q: What did he ask the Roman general for?
review.why: The story says he asked for Yavneh and its sages, for Rabban Gamliel's family, and for a doctor for Rabbi Zadok.

review.q: Who gathered the Oral Torah into the Mishnah?
review.why: Rabbi Judah the Prince, called Rabbi, gathered the Mishnah in about 200 CE.

review.q: Which list gives the six orders of the Mishnah?
choices: Seeds, Festivals, Women, Damages, Holy Things, Purities
Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua
Berakhot, Shabbat, Sukkah, Pesachim, Avot, Sanhedrin
Moses, Joshua, elders, prophets, pairs, rabbis
review.why: The six orders are Seeds, Festivals, Women, Damages, Holy Things and Purities. The second list is Bible books; the third is tractates.

review.q: How many tractates does the Mishnah have?
review.why: The Mishnah has sixty-three tractates in six orders. Thirty-nine is the number of kinds of Shabbat work.
The Mishnah is written in short, clear Hebrew sentences that state rules and record who disagreed.

review.q: What grew out of the Mishnah to make the Talmud?
review.why: The Gemara is the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah. Mishnah plus Gemara equals Talmud.

review.q: Which rule shows mercy built into the Mishnah's law?
choices: A worker must be paid on time
A sukkah may not be over twenty cubits tall
The evening Shema is said until midnight
Priests eat their offering at nightfall
review.why: Paying a worker on time protects the worker. The other rules are about festival and prayer times, not mercy.
